study.title: Ezekiel 16 - Jerusalem, the infidelity, and the restoration of the covenant
study.overview: This chapter uses a strong and uncomfortable allegory to expose the gravity of Jerusalem's sin. The city is described as an abandoned child that God rescues, makes it grow, embellishment and honor, but then transforms the gifts received into instruments of infidelity. The main image is that of spiritual adultery: Jerusalem exchanges the Lord for idols, corrupts worship, perverts justice and reaches the point of sacrificing his own children. Still, the chapter ends with a note of mercy: God promises to remember his covenant, restore and bring shameful repentance, without denying the seriousness of guilt.

outline.title: Jerusalem: From the Forebearing to God's Intakement
outline.explanation: The prophet begins with the humiliating origin of the city, as a child without care, and shows the gracious action of the Lord, who makes her live, grow, washed, dressed, adorned and known for her beauty. All that Jerusalem has good is presented as a gift received, not as self merit.

outline.title: Infidelity: idolatry, corruption and violence
outline.explanation: Jerusalem uses beauty and the goods received to prostitute himself, that is, to seek other gods and ungodly covenants. The text extends the accusation showing the surrender to idols, the corruption of worship, the profanity of what God gave and the sacrifice of children. The image becomes harder to show the depth of apostasy.

outline.title: Unavoidable trial and shameful comparison
outline.explanation: The Lord announces that the nakedness of the city will be exposed, his allies will turn against it and her guilt will be punished publicly. Jerusalem is compared to adulterestheans and murderers, and even Sodom and Samaria enter as a mirror of shame: instead of judging others, Jerusalem has proved even worse.

outline.title: Memory of alliance and final restoration
outline.explanation: After the sentence, God states that he will act according to the broken covenant, but he will also remember his old covenant and establish an eternal covenant. The end is not the denial of sin, but the reconciliation that produces remembrance, shame and silence before the grace received.

study.context: Ezekiel speaks to the covenant community in a national judgment scenario. The chapter itself addresses Jerusalem as a representative of God's people. The notes highlight that the purpose of the message is to convince and humiliate, not soften sin. The prophet uses a socially shocking allegory to make visible the divine repulse for idolatry and injustice. It is not necessary to suppose more than the text and the notes allow: Jerusalem symbolizes the people of the covenant, and their behavior is described with the language of spiritual adultery to show the gravity of the rupture with God.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the grace received increases, and does not diminish, spiritual responsibility. Jerusalem did not fall for a lack of divine favor; on the contrary, it was lifted up by God, and then used gifts received to exalt and corrupt itself. Idolatry appears as adultery against the Lord, because the people exchange the faithfulness of the covenant for other loves. The text also shows that sin is not only ritual: it reaches heart, worship, relations and social justice, reaching the shedding of innocent blood. At the same time, the last word of God is not only destruction. He judges with justice, but also promises to remember his covenant and work reconciliation. This restoration does not automatically absolve sin; it produces holy shame, memory and breaking before divine mercy. In Protestant evangelical reading, the chapter harmonizes with the doctrine of sovereign grace: God is the initiator of good, the judge of sin and the restorer of his people.

scholarViews.insight: Tyndale points out that Jerusalem is deliberately expelled to the people to understand the uglity of their sin and recognize the righteousness of divine judgment.
Matthew Henry notes that Jerusalem is remembered of his miserable, abandoned and destined to death origin to show that his life came entirely from God's compassion.
Adam Clarke notes that the final passage points to restoration to God's favor after correction, understanding the promise as a sign of renewal of the covenant and divine mercy.

questions: What does this chapter reveal about the relationship between God's gifts and human responsibility before them?
In what ways does the image of spiritual adultery help to understand the gravity of idolatry and unfaithfulness to the Lord?
How does the end of the chapter correct a vision that sees only judgment, without realizing God's faithfulness to his covenant?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a spiritual mirror and not just as historical denunciation. Ask where you have used gifts from God - time, resources, influence, abilities - to exalt other faithfulness in the place of fidelity to the Lord. Confess concrete sins of ingratitude, idolatry, and self-reliance. At the same time, receive the hope that God will not abandon his covenant: take seriously the shame of sin, but do not doubt the possibility of real repentance and restoration by God's mercy. A concrete practice is to write three areas in which you received much from God and, alongside each one, record a corresponding obedient answer for this week.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not clarify all the historical and symbolic details of the allegory, so the reading was maintained within what the text itself and the commentators cited claim. There are also interpretive observations in the notes, especially on the exact scope of the final restoration; therefore, the application was presented as an evangelical reading, not as an undeniable conclusion about each image of the chapter.
